summary: DHCP servers have grown well beyond the base specifications, and one such feature is context-specific configuration, where clients get different settings depending on where they are in the network. This informational memo describes some of these features and explains how they operate.

eli5.summary: A hotel can give guests different Wi-Fi instructions depending on the floor they are on. This describes how address-giving servers can hand out different settings based on where a device plugs in.

questions: how dhcp servers choose options by location
how does dhcp know which subnet a client is on
what is a dhcp relay agent
subtitle: How DHCP servers use relay information to hand out different settings depending on where a client is attached.

tldr.problem: DHCP was meant to give each device configuration suited to its location in the network, but how servers actually do this was never documented.
tldr.mechanism: The server works out the client's link from the relay agent's address or relay-supplied identifiers, then picks the matching subnet and options; shared subnets and client classification handle harder cases.
tldr.outcome: The memo records existing practice for operators and protocol designers. It adds no new protocol, and its security section warns that a client could misrepresent where it is attached.

today: RFC 7969 is an Informational memo, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It records practice as of October 2016 rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Location-Specific Configuration
sections.content:
DHCP does more than hand out addresses. It also provisions things like DNS server addresses and default search domains. The authors of the DHCP specifications intended servers to provision each device with configuration appropriate to its location in the network, but the practice was never documented in detail.

Existing DHCP servers do provide such capabilities. This memo describes them for the benefit of operators and of protocol designers who may want to use DHCP to configure their own services.
sections.eli5: Where you are matters. A device plugged in on one side of a building may need different settings than one on the other side.

sections.title: How a Server Finds the Client's Link
sections.content:
A client that does not yet have a routable IP address cannot reach an off-link server, so it talks to a relay agent on its local link. The relay, which has a routable address, forwards the request to the server directly or through other relays. The server typically uses the relay's client-facing IP address to find the client's point of attachment and choose the matching subnet- or link-specific configuration. Clients on the server's own link need no relay.

In DHCPv4 the relay sets the giaddr field and may add a relay agent option (RFC 3046). Helpful sub-options include Link Selection (RFC 3527) and Virtual Subnet Selection (RFC 6607), and a client may request a subnet with the option in RFC 3011.

In DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) the server can use the link-address field of Relay-forward messages, which needs an address larger than link-local on the relay. Otherwise the relay can add an Interface-ID option, which is useful only if the values are unique within the administrative domain. Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agents (RFC 6221) set link-address to :: and supply an Interface-ID for finer location detail.
sections.eli5: A helper on each street tells the server which street the request came from. The server then knows which settings to send back.

sections.title: Worked Configuration Examples
sections.content:
Using a hypothetical JSON configuration syntax (the RFC knows of no server using this exact format), the memo shows two cases. In a simple subnetted network, each link has its own prefix with a routers option, because in IPv4 the default route is typically set by DHCP and differs per link. The server finds the prefix enclosing the link-identifying address and returns that prefix's options. A client on Link A, in 192.0.2.0/26, gets router 192.0.2.1.

In the regional example, an ISP wants devices to use servers local to their region so traffic does not cross regions needlessly. The server maps the link-identifying address to a link, the link to a region, and the region to options such as a SIP Server and DNS Recursive Name Server. It resolves the listed names and may cache the answers, as discussed in RFC 7227.

The memo also notes that a relay agent can run on any IP node, not just a router, and that relays can be cascaded.
sections.eli5: The server keeps a list: this street gets these settings, and this neighborhood uses these nearby helpers. It looks up where you are and reads off the right line.

sections.title: Cascaded Relays and Shared Subnets
sections.content:
In DHCPv4 with cascaded relays, only the first relay sets giaddr, and later relays leave it alone, so the reply returns to the first relay while the request travelled the full chain. DHCPv6 is more structured: each relay encapsulates the message, there may be up to 32 levels, and every relay can add its own options so it is clear which relay inserted which.

Sometimes more than one subnet of the same protocol family lives on one link, called shared subnets in Unix environments, multinet on Windows and DHCP Superscope in Microsoft servers. Use cases include renumbering, running out of space, allocating from a prefix different from the relay's own, and cable networks where modems and user devices get separate address spaces.

Topology alone cannot choose the subnet there, so servers use client classification, sorting packets into classes by option presence or values. The details are implementation dependent and not part of DHCPv4 or DHCPv6.
sections.eli5: If two groups share one street, the server also checks a name tag on each device to decide which group it belongs to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker could misrepresent its point of attachment, causing the server to give out addresses, prefixes and options for a different place, which can leak information about services in parts of the network the attacker cannot reach. Suggested defenses: filter DHCP traffic at administrative domain boundaries, have servers ignore requests from unknown subnets, and use relays that validate messages. For instance, a CMTS can check that the chaddr MAC address matches the cable modem it came from. Relays and servers directly connected to clients can reject traffic that looks as if it passed a relay.

The memo adds that current DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 standards lack strong cryptographic protection, and points to RFC 7610 (DHCPv6-Shield) against rogue servers, and to RFC 7819, RFC 7824 and RFC 7844 for privacy.
sections.eli5: Someone could lie about where they are plugged in to get settings meant for somewhere else. Checking who is allowed to talk to the server helps.
